title: What the Water Knew
blurb: Dagny wakes to water that runs uphill to her feet, and the one man who can name it has never seen anyone come back.

blocks.text: The water from my washbasin ran uphill.

I'd caught the basin with my elbow getting out of bed, because my arms didn't know yet how heavy the rest of me was. It went over. The water hit the floorboards and should have run to the window, where the floor drops. Every spill in our back room has run to the window since I was six. This one didn't. It ran the other way, up the slope, round the leg of the chair, and stopped against my bare feet.
It was cold. I stood in it and couldn't make myself move.

Then I tried everything I could think of. I stepped round to the far side of the puddle, and the water turned and came after me in a thin line until it touched my heels again. I stepped back, past an arm's length, and it stopped, lay flat, and spread toward the window the way water should. I stepped in again. It came again.

I took the door key off the string round my neck and held the string out at arm's length. The key hung straight. I brought it in close to my chest, and the key tilted a finger's width toward me and stayed there, with nothing pulling it but me.

I counted under my breath, because my hands had started to shake. Six stone four of carry at the last bell. Ten hours flat on the bed since. Ten hours should take two and a half stone off. That leaves three stone eleven, near enough: slow and sore, but able to play. My knees said more than that. My knees said nearer five. Five is one stone off Heavy. Ten is a cracked bone.

"I'm frightened," I said, out loud, to nobody, because there was nobody else in the room to say it to. My voice came out small. I said it again, so it would be true in the room and not just stuck in my throat.

Then I got the floor cloth and knelt down in the water, which took a long time and hurt my knees, and mopped it up before Rafe woke. Every time I wrung the cloth into the basin, the drips ran back across the boards to me.
Rafe hadn't been to bed. He was at the kitchen table in his match jacket with a slip of paper flat under both hands, as if it might blow away.
"Dags. Sit down before you fall down, will you?"
I sat. It took me two goes.
"Are you all right?" he said.
"I'm counted," I said. It was my father's call for a checked cage, and Rafe knew it, and he let it be.
He looked at the slip. Then he tried to smile. "You know what Teague's book is, Dags? It's a shaft with no Pins and a lid on top. You go in, and there's only one way to go, isn't there?"
"Rafe. What happened?"
He went still. Rafe is never still. When he's caught out, he goes still and says things exactly as they are, like a boy reading off a board.

"I went up to collect. Teague's man turned the slip over and read me the back. 'Any match with an unregistered player on either side is void. Stakes held by the book.' I read it four times after. It said the same thing every time."
My throat shut. It shut the way it does when you swallow something too big, and it stayed shut.

Unregistered player. The Weighman had written it in the league book beside my name with his own pen. Emergency clause. The league would let the win stand if I registered inside seven days. Teague's book didn't care about the league.
"So I still owe him eighty," Rafe said. "It's eighty-four by the next match. He said it would be a shame."
"It was me," I said. "I was the unregistered player."
"You were the only Anchor we had. Wat walked. You went down because nobody else would, didn't you? It's not your fault."

I didn't answer him, because it was. He knew half of it. He didn't know the other half: that three weeks ago I'd sat at this same table and worked out the Ninepins' odds on a coal chit and left it by the bread where he'd find it. I'd put the bet in his head. Then I'd gone down the shaft unregistered and voided it. I hadn't even earned a fee for it. An unregistered Anchor gets nothing for a win, so there weren't even five crowns to put in his hand.
"Did you know about the back of the slip?" I asked.
He was quiet for a moment. "It's on the back of every slip," he said.

I wanted him to stop looking like that, so I said the only thing I could think of. "Teague's Tallymen couldn't find the bottom of a well with a lamp and a map, Rafe. We'll play them before the Step, and he can watch."
He laughed, a little, and his shoulders came down.

It cost me. I had to keep my face easy while my chest felt like someone was standing on it, and when he went out, I put my head down on the table and stayed there until the cold went out of my hands. It was guilt. I could call it something else, but it was guilt, and it sat under my breastbone all that day and all the next. I love my brother. I'd done this to him twice.

On the third day I could walk to Shaft Nine without stopping, but only just. Osk was already on the Lip in his chair beside the ladder, and when he saw how I came across the yard, he said, "You sit. You're still carrying."

So I sat on a plank by the Lid rail and watched the others rig the ropes. Lisbet went down first, fast, calling "Move, Dunnet, move," and Dunnet went down after her, booming at nothing. Hal went last, slow, with his hand pressed flat to his side. Pru stood on the platform with her chalk board. Then they were all below the L1 lamp, and it was only me and Osk on the Lip.
"Quillon," he said. "Come here. Bring the plank."
I dragged it a couple of strides closer and sat down again. He didn't look at me. He looked at my boots.
"Look," he said. He waited. "At your boot."
There was loose grit on the planks, there always is. It was moving. It was sliding across the wood toward my boot in little lines, slowly, and stopping against the leather.
"How long?" he said.
"Since the last bell."
"Did you do... the Release?"
"I don't know what that is."
He shut his eyes. He sat like that long enough for me to hear Pru calling odds down the shaft.
"Then you're... leaning."
I knew the word. Every Anchor knows the word. I'd just never thought it would be mine.

"The league will tell you it's rare," Osk said. "They'll tell you it's looked after. Leaning Anchors are retired to care in the Settle. That's the line." He stopped, and the stop was long. "I've been round shafts all my life, Dagny. I have never... seen one come back."

The cold came into the lining of my father's coat. It came in at the back of my neck and went down my spine and into my hands, and I put my right hand in my pocket next to my bad one so he wouldn't see them shake.

"Listen, now," he said. "One. It puts weight on you. A stone a week. An ounce an hour, near enough, waking or sleeping. Two. Ordinary ground won't take it off you. Lying flat will drain your match carry, but at half what it should, and it won't touch the lean. Nothing in Scarrow takes a lean off you, outside the Settle."
Half. So my knees had been right. I'd been carrying nearer five stone that first morning, not three.

"Three," he said. He waited. "There's a... rule. Rule nine. An Anchor found leaning by plumb-bob is struck off the register. What you've played stands. What you're owed..." He let that one hang longest of all. "...is forfeit. Fees, purse, all of it, to the league. And the league sends you to the Settle."

I counted it. Five crowns a win, if I registered. Prize share of the Step purse, if we ever got there. All of it was what Rafe needed, and all of it was forfeit the day somebody held a bob near me. And a stone a week, every week, on top of anything I carried in a match. In six weeks I'd be Heavy without gripping a Pin at all. In ten I'd be at a cracked bone just from standing still.
"Is there any way to be rid of it?" I asked. My voice wasn't steady and I didn't try to make it steady.

He was quiet a while. "There's old lore. Throwing. You stand in the mark, unaided, and grip a Pin nobody's holding, and you do the Release. The lean leaves you for the Pin. It holds a set with no hand on it for ten counts, along the line from the Pin to you, and then it goes true. Once. You can throw a lean once."
"Then I could..."
"Not yet. A light lean won't throw. It needs weight behind it. Six stone of it." He looked at me at last. "By the time it will throw, girl, you won't climb a ladder."
Six stone. Six weeks. The Step was week eight.
"And you never do it in front of a Weighman," he said. "Never. Every soul on the Lip sees a Pin set with no hand on it. Then they come with the bob."
"Who else knows?" I said.

"Nobody. And nobody else learns it from you. Not Hal. Not your brother." He leaned forward in the chair, as far as his spine let him, which wasn't far. "Now. The Release. So you never make it worse. If you let go wrong again after a big hold, it doesn't make a second lean. It doubles the one you've got."

He taught it the way he teaches everything, in steps. One: breathe in through the nose, all the way down, until your belly's full. Two: hold the breath and feel the Pin go quiet in your hand. Three: let the breath out and the hand with it, together, finger by finger, the little finger last. Three counts. That's all it is. Three counts, and nobody had taught them to me before I went down the shaft.

"Again," he said, and I did it with my hand on the plank. "Again." I did it twenty times, and my hand learned it, and my chest stayed tight the whole time, because a thing that takes three counts to learn shouldn't cost a person a stone a week for the rest of her life.

On the fifth day Lisbet slung me down to L1 and I practised it on a real Pin. I gripped and held true down, which costs nothing, and did the Release, and gripped again, and did it again. Chalk dust from the mark drifted in toward my boots while I worked. Every few minutes I scuffed it flat so Hal wouldn't see it from L3.
"Steady," Hal said once, from below. He meant my grip. He didn't mean it kindly. He coughed after it, and I heard him stop the cough halfway.
Then they drilled the catch. Lisbet swung the practice sack across the shaft to Dunnet, and Pru called it from the Lip, fast, the way she calls a live Drop. "Long wall, evens, evens, now!"
On "now", Dunnet's hands opened. The sack went straight past him and down into the Throat with a thump.
He laughed. It was his big laugh, the one you can hear in the yard. It went on a breath longer than the miss was worth. Then a breath longer than that.
"Butterfingers Haig," he said. "Sorry, Pru. Sorry, Counts. Again."

It was nothing. Everybody fumbles. But he'd fumbled on the exact word Pru called, not before it and not after, and I'm the one who notices things like that. I filed it the way I file a reading, and I didn't like the feeling of filing it, because I liked Dunnet.
Lisbet swung out next, for the rope end on the far wall by L2. She reached for it and missed it by an arm's length, and swung back, and caught the wall with her shoulder.
"That lamp's smoking," she said. "I can't see a thing past the middle."
I looked at the L2 lamp. It was burning clean and bright. I didn't say anything.

On the sixth day Rafe walked me to the league office at the back of the Weighhouse yard. He waited outside on the step. The clerk was a thin man with ink on his cuffs and a scale in the corner of the room.
"Quillon, Dagny. Shaft Nine. Anchor," he said, writing. "Weight as you stand. On you go."

I stood on it. I didn't look at the dial. I watched his pen instead. I knew there was still about a stone of the match in my bones, near enough, because half-rate drain is slow and I'd lain flat every hour I could and it still wasn't gone. He wrote the number in the column headed BASE.
I opened my mouth to tell him I hadn't drained. Then I shut it. An Anchor who hasn't drained in five days gets asked why. I wanted to be out of that room without anybody asking me anything.

"Good," the clerk said. "Now, you played under the emergency clause, so you're due tomorrow. Seven days from the match." He slid a card across the desk. "Can't finish you without a medical. Settle medical, first thing tomorrow. Bones and balance."
The Settle. My father ran the Settle lift. It's where his cable parted. My knees went soft and I put my right hand flat on the desk.
"Standard," the clerk said, not looking up. "Doctor stands every new Anchor next to the plumb-bob. It's in the room with the scale."
I could see Rafe through the glass of the door, waiting for me, with his collar up and his hands in his pockets, eighty-four crowns of trouble on a boy of sixteen.
"Cage going down, Da," I said under my breath. "Hold the brake."
Tomorrow I had to stand next to a string with a weight on it, and if it leaned toward me, it would take my fees, and my name, and the only money my brother had left to hope for.
